title: Coaching Case Studies #2
author: Craig Barton
summary: Two more coaching write-ups, both turning on a hypothesis Barton forms while observing and then tests with evidence. In the first, a teacher's explanation of the relationship between the volumes of a cone and a cylinder is genuinely excellent, but Barton suspects students do not know what they are supposed to be doing while it happens. He photographs the room, showing that at least half the class is copying while listening - a dual task that is hard in itself and, worse, means heads are down during the gesturing that directs attention to the critical step. The fix is trivially small and entirely procedural: state before each explanation that this is a watching, listening and thinking phase, empty hands and eyes front, with copying deferred. The second case is about a well-meant hint. Before a Do Now question the teacher warns of a hidden pair of brackets; nearly every mini-whiteboard comes back correct and the class moves on. Barton's point is that the hint invalidated the check - asked afterwards, some students said they would have managed without it and some said they would not. The coaching conclusion is to withhold support until after the check, then respond, possibly with the same hint, and check again.
points: Barton's method is worth noting independently of its findings: he forms an explicit hypothesis during observation and then gathers evidence, such as a photograph of the class, to test it in the coaching conversation.
A brilliant explanation can still fail if students have not been told what to do during it, because listening while copying means missing the gestures that carry the critical part.
The fix is procedural rather than pedagogical - eyes front, empty hands, copying later - which makes it cheap to adopt and easy to repeat before every explanation.
A hint given before a check for understanding destroys the check's diagnostic value, since success afterwards tells you nothing about how secure the knowledge was.
Barton's resequencing keeps the hint available but moves it after the data: check first, then respond with the hint or a student explanation, then check again.
quotes: But I formed a hypothesis: the students did not know what they were supposed to be doing during this explanation. Should they be watching and listening, or should they also be trying to copy down the working out from the board?

I took some pictures of the class to illustrate that at least half of the students were attempting to copy whilst listening. Not only is listening whilst writing really tricky, but the moments where students had their heads down writing meant that they missed the really important gesturing that the teacher was doing at the board to focus attention on the critical part of the explanation.

This led to a nice and simple fix: before each explanation, the teacher will make it clear to students that they should be watching, listening and thinking - empty hands and eyes on the front. This will allow them to get the most from the explanation. The copying down can come later.

The students then wrote their answers on their mini-whiteboards and almost everyone got the answer correct. The teacher was happy that understanding was secure, and moved on to the next phase of the lesson.

My hypothesis was that they might not have been able to get the answer correct without that hint. As no time machine was available, the only way I could test this was to ask a few of the students if they would have got that question correct without the hint. Some said they would, others said they wouldn’t.

As teachers, it is our job to help our students understand and feel successful, so if we foresee where they might struggle it is very hard to resist giving them some guidance. But - and it is a big but - if we do this before a check for understanding, it invalidates our check for understanding as we have no way of knowing how secure that knowledge was before the hint.
